subject: business-studies
title: Payback and ARR
welcome_lead: Two quick yardsticks for screening investments.
meta_desc: A-Level Investment Appraisal: payback period and accounting rate of return.
final_note: Payback is fast and intuitive; ARR captures profitability over the life.

concepts.def: Time taken for cash inflows to repay the initial outlay.
Average annual profit divided by initial investment, times 100.
Cash spent at the start of the project.
Net profit each year from the project.
Payback prioritises getting cash back quickly.

walkthroughs.body_html: Add cumulative cash flows year by year until they equal the initial outlay. Project cost 100, inflows of 40 then 40 then 40 - payback occurs in year 3 (at 2.5 years).
ARR = average annual profit / initial investment x 100. Easy to calculate from accounts but ignores the timing of profits - a serious weakness.
Firms use payback for cash-tight contexts and risky projects, ARR for comparing profitability quickly, and NPV for serious investment decisions.

mcqs.q: Why can a profitable business still fail?
options: Because cash flow and profit are different — a business may be profitable on paper but run out of cash to pay bills, especially if customers owe money or stock ties up funds.
Gross profit is profit before VAT and net profit is profit after VAT.
Profitable businesses fail only when employees steal.
If a business is profitable it cannot run out of money.

mcqs.q: What is the difference between gross profit and net profit?
options: Cash flow only matters at year-end.
Gross profit = revenue minus cost of goods sold (direct costs only); net profit = revenue minus ALL costs including overheads, interest and tax. Net profit is the bottom line.
Gross profit is profit before VAT and net profit is profit after VAT.
Gross profit and net profit are the same thing.

mcqs.q: Why are cash flow and profit different on different time-scales?
options: Cash flow only matters at year-end.

Profit is recognised when a sale is made (even on credit); cash flow is when money actually moves. A profitable sale today may produce no cash for 60 days while bills are due — creating a cash-flow problem despite profit.
Cash flow and profit are the same thing measured differently.
Gross profit is profit before VAT and net profit is profit after VAT.
